articles.title: Astronomers find ‘reborn’ planet around a dead star
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Astronomers have identified what could be the first second-generation planet found around a white dwarf, a dead star that has exhausted its
articles.body: BENGALURU: Astronomers have identified what could be the first second-generation planet found around a white dwarf, a dead star that has exhausted its fuel. The planet appears to have formed from material the star itself threw into space as it died.The discovery was made by a team led by the University of Warwick and centres on a white dwarf called “HS 0209+0832”. Its atmosphere contains unusually high levels of heavy elements including zinc, copper and, most notably, niobium, which was found at levels more than 1,000 times higher than in the Sun.These are all elements created during the death of a star, as per a statement shared with TOI. Niobium has not previously been detected in a white dwarf. The unusual chemical mix provided the key clue. Nicholas Stone, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, said the pattern was a signature of the “s-process”, a nuclear reaction that builds heavy elements inside dying stars.“It’s a chemical signature no ordinary, ‘first-generation’ planet should carry, which told us that this new planet was something different,” he said. Researchers believe the white dwarf is feeding on a newly formed giant planet.As the star died, it expelled material that may have gathered into a disc around it. A planet could then have formed from this disc, making it a second-generation world. Such planet formation is not straightforward. Material expelled by a dying star would normally escape rather than settle into orbit.Jamie Williams, a PhD student at the University of Warwick and the study’s first author, said the star probably needed a companion that pulled some of the expelled material back into orbit.“Second-generation planets are worlds that form out of the material a star casts off as it dies. They’re incredibly rare, and finding one around a white dwarf was completely unexpected. It’s a bit like finding a planet that has risen from the ashes of the very star it once orbited,” Williams said.Further evidence came from Nasa’s TESS satellite, which detected a faint change in brightness repeating every 4.4 days. This is consistent with a Jupiter-sized gas giant in a close orbit around the white dwarf.The planet is so close to the white dwarf that its outer atmosphere is expected to be boiling away under the intense radiation. Some of this escaping material could be falling on to the white dwarf, producing the unusual chemical signature observed by astronomers.If confirmed, “HS 0209+0832” would be the first white dwarf known to host a second-generation planet. The discovery could also help astronomers search for more such “reborn” worlds around other dead stars.The findings of the astronomers, funded by the European Research Council (ERC), have been published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

articles.title: Scientists examined 13 insects trapped in 99-million-year-old amber and identified a new species whose flexible mouthpart reached nearly twice its body length, possibly letting it probe deep into tree bark for sap
articles.summary: Not much in the world has survived to be known as old as the dinosaurs, but when it comes to a recently discovered insect species, the statement holds
articles.body: Not much in the world has survived to be known as old as the dinosaurs, but when it comes to a recently discovered insect species, the statement holds true. Some 99 million years ago, a tiny insect belonging to a previously unknown species became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber; the fossil preserved within it has now led a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describe a new species named Cretodorus noonoo, or 'Noo-Noo'.The researchers examined insect fossils belonging to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar. The study published in the journal Insects, also revealed an extraordinary biological adaptation that characterised Noo-Noo and its close relatives, exceptionally long and flexible mouthparts that were twice the length of their body. The researchers believe that this unusual structure enabled the insects to reach food sources that were inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts, deep inside cracks and crevices in tree bark. In their modern relatives, the mouthparts are structured like a simple needle, allowing them to pierce plant tissues and suck fluids from them.Unique mouthparts that no longer existThe ancient insects examined were found to possess extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds. Using high-resolution micro-computed tomography, the researchers were able to reconstruct their internal structure. The scans showed that the folds were not merely external ornamentation but part of the structure itself. They likely gave the mouthparts flexibility while preventing them from kinking or collapsing, much like a bendy drinking straw or a corrugated flexible hose.In some of the preserved fossils, the mouthparts were preserved in a bent position. Because the amber froze the insects in place when they became trapped in the resin, the researchers view this as further evidence that the mouthparts were also flexible during the insects' lifetimes. Such a structure is unknown among their living relatives today, pointing to an ancient evolutionary solution that has since disappeared.The mouthparts of "Noo-Noo" pointed backwards and functioned as a piercing-and-sucking system that, like the mouthparts of their modern relatives, was less suitable for feeding on nectar. Moreover, despite examining numerous fossils, the researchers found no convincing evidence of pollen accumulating on their bodies, a sign that would have indicated a role as pollinators.According to an explanation proposed by the researchers, these insects were specialists in sucking sap from trees. Their long, flexible mouthparts could have snaked through narrow cracks in the bark and guided the piercing organs toward the deep vascular tissues.At the tip was another unusual feature: a structure with two grooved lobes that likely opened during feeding, helping to anchor the mouthpart to the walls of the crack, much like a wall anchor expanding inside a drilled hole.The forests and insects of the timeThe researchers' discovery may also have broader significance for the understanding of Cretaceous forests. Long or corrugated feeding structures appeared in several unrelated insect groups during this period, raising the possibility that forests rich in thick-barked trees provided an advantage for insects capable of reaching deeper tissues.The study notes that resin-producing forests of the Cretaceous period were also associated with evidence of recurrent fires and that trees in fire-prone environments often develop thicker bark. The researchers cautiously suggest that such conditions may have created ecological opportunities for unique feeding strategies, ones that are almost entirely absent among planthoppers today."The discovery of 'Noo-Noo,' a new species that lived approximately 99 million years ago, gives us an extraordinary glimpse into the insect world of the age of the dinosaurs. This is not merely an insect previously unknown to science, but an animal that developed an evolutionary solution with almost no modern equivalent: a long, flexible and durable feeding organ that likely enabled it to reach food deep within tree bark," said Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, one of the study authors."The fact that similar structures appeared in several insect groups during the Cretaceous period suggests that ancient forests created ecological conditions and opportunities very different from those we know today. The discovery of a new species like this is therefore not simply the addition of another name to the tree of life, but another piece of the puzzle that enables us to reconstruct what ecosystems looked like and how they functioned tens of millions of years ago," they added.

articles.title: Meet Rye Lynn Rost: The Montana 7th grader who compared banana and plantain starch to make stronger bioplastic
articles.summary: A seventh grader in Montana compared banana and plantain starch to develop a stronger bioplastic.
articles.body: A seventh grader in Montana compared banana and plantain starch to develop a stronger bioplastic. Rye Lynn Rost, a student at Baker Junior High School in Baker, MT, wanted to create plastics from natural materials that could break down without losing their durability too quickly.For her project, she studied bioplastics made from plantains (Musa paradisiaca) and bananas (Musa acuminata). She examined amyloplasts (plant cells that make and store starch) and measured the starch content of both fruits.According to the Society for Science, Rye found that plantains had more amyloplasts and starch. Their bioplastic also had higher tensile strength and breaking distance than the banana version.Rye compares bananas and plantains to make stronger bioplasticsRye said, “While there are many issues in the world that we can use STEM to solve, plastic pollution is the one that concerns me the most”. She explained that bioplastics are made from natural materials and can break down over time. However, she did not want them to break down too quickly.Rye said, “Bioplastics must withstand water, sunlight, and other environmental conditions without breaking down or losing durability”. She decided to compare bioplastics made from plantains (Musa Paradisiaca) and bananas (Musa acuminata). The two fruits are closely related, but plantains have thicker skin and more starch.What did Rye’s tests reveal about banana and plantain bioplasticsRye began by comparing the amyloplasts found in bananas and plantains. She extracted individual cells from both fruits and counted the amyloplasts in 100 cells from each. She then extracted the starch from each fruit and measured the amount present per gram.After examining the cells and starch, she made bioplastic from both bananas and plantains and compared the results with plastic parafilm. The tests showed that plantains had the highest number of amyloplasts and the most starch.Rye then tested both bioplastics for strength and stretch. The plantain bioplastic had higher tensile strength and breaking distance than the banana bioplastic, which makes it stronger.Plantain bioplastic shows greater strength than banana versionThe plantain bioplastic performed better than the banana bioplastic in the strength tests. Rye found that the plantain bioplastic had higher tensile strength and breaking distance. This made the plantain version a stronger plastic than the banana bioplastic.Her results followed her earlier findings that plantains had the highest number of amyloplasts and the most starch. Rye also compared the bioplastics with plastic parafilm as part of her testing. The project aimed to develop a bioplastic that could break down while remaining durable under environmental conditions.Rye Lynn Rost’s journey from 4H to materials scienceRye is a member of 4H and has presented a cow, goat, cat, pig, and poultry at the fair. She takes care of 14 goats and has also helped train cows and pigs. Rye has high-frequency hearing loss and wears hearing aids.She said, “Everyone was worried that I would do badly in school, but I have gotten straight As my whole life”.She wants to become a materials scientist and wants to develop better bioplastics. Her long-term goal is to create the right recipe for different types of single-use plastics.

articles.title: Scientists studying ancient Siberian bone fragments used DNA to identify a previously unknown extinct bovine related to modern yaks that followed its own evolutionary path for hundreds of thousands of years
articles.summary: A handful of unremarkable bone fragments from caves in southern Siberia have turned out to hold an extraordinary evolutionary story.
articles.body: A handful of unremarkable bone fragments from caves in southern Siberia have turned out to hold an extraordinary evolutionary story. According to an online report by Phys Org, ancient DNA recovered from the remains has revealed a previously unknown bovine species that lived across the region for hundreds of thousands of years and shared a distant ancestry with modern yaks. The discovery, published in Current Biology, adds another chapter to the complex history of Ice Age biodiversity in the Altai region.A species hidden in small bonesThe discovery emerged from fragments recovered from Denisova Cave and other archaeological sites across southern Siberia. Many of the bones were too incomplete or poorly preserved to identify by appearance alone. Genetic analysis, however, offered a much clearer picture, claims the online report.Researchers from the Center for Paleogenetics in Stockholm, the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the University of Vienna analyzed 20 ancient genomes spanning roughly 200,000 years. Comparison of these genomes with those of modern and extinct bovines revealed that the remains represented a previously unrecognized lineage. The animal was related to modern yaks but had followed an independent evolutionary trajectory for a remarkably long period. Genetic evidence suggests that its lineage began separating from that of modern yaks around 400,000 years ago and became fully distinct roughly 250,000 years ago, the Phys Org report adds.Climate may have influenced its evolutionThe timing of the split provides clues about how climate affected the evolution of the species. Around 400,000 years ago, the region experienced a particularly strong warm climatic period. Changes in temperature and habitat may have separated populations, eventually allowing them to evolve independently.The comparison is striking because the estimated age of this divergence is similar to the period when brown bears and polar bears are thought to have begun following separate evolutionary paths, the report adds.The genetic record also points to another major environmental shift. During the last interglacial warm period, around 120,000 years ago, the newly identified bovine appears to have undergone a population replacement accompanied by declining genetic diversity. For an animal adapted to cold conditions, prolonged warming may have created significant ecological pressure.Another mystery from the AltaiThe discovery adds to the growing reputation of the Altai region as an important refuge for biodiversity during repeated Ice Age cycles. Denisova Cave has already produced evidence of Denisovans, an archaic human population identified through genetic analysis of fossil remains.The new bovine discovery reveals the region’s significance extended way beyond human evolution. It may have served as a long-term refuge where animal populations survived dramatic climatic fluctuations and developed into distinct lineages.Interestingly, researchers found little evidence that the newly identified bovine interbred with other large bovines living in the region, including steppe bison and aurochs, the wild ancestors of modern cattle.An extinction still shrouded in mysteryThe youngest specimen examined in the study dates to around 27,000 years ago. The species disappeared sometime after that, but researchers cannot yet determine exactly when or why it became extinct. Modern wild yaks are now restricted largely to high-elevation areas of the Tibetan Plateau, making the Siberian lineage a fascinating reminder of how much broader the historical range of yak-like animals once was.For now, the species remains without a formal scientific name. DNA evidence can reveal its evolutionary identity, but researchers need to compare the genetic findings with previously described yak-like fossils from the region before determining whether those remains belong to the same animal. Further work could eventually put a name, appearance and clearer ecological history to this long-lost Siberian bovine.Images Courtesy: Phys Org

articles.title: The planetary wave headed for California isn’t what you think it is
articles.summary: A particularly severe El Niño will raise sea levels, making storms and flooding more dangerous.
articles.body: A rather strong “planetary wave” recently slammed into South America and is making its way toward California. In case you’re worried about headlines warning of the supposedly “freak” phenomenon “bringing trouble,” it’s worth understanding what this wave really is and isn’t. Called a Kelvin wave, it’s carrying warm water to the Americas that’s typically trapped farther west. That’s raising sea levels along already vulnerable coastlines. These kinds of waves are common. When they do arrive, they can exacerbate existing problems. And this particular Kelvin wave could have more dramatic consequences than usual. But “If you’re going to be out there looking for it, you’re not going to see it,” says Richard Seager, a research professor at Columbia University’s Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory. A photo accompanying The New York Times’ reporting on the Kelvin wave, depicting a surface wave smashing into someone’s beachfront condominium, is misleading, he notes. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says a Kelvin wave is more like “waves in your bathtub, which slowly slosh around.” Water levels rise and fall in peaks and valleys, but they’re not breaking violently against a shore. Kelvin waves are a typical signal of an El Niño, although they can also take place during other phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) pattern. During other phases, trade winds over the Pacific Ocean push warm waters near South America westward toward Asia. That causes an “upwelling,” pulling cooler water from below up toward the surface of the ocean along the equator. As a result, the eastern equatorial Pacific is typically cool, while the western equatorial Pacific is warm. During an El Niño, those trade winds die down, allowing the warm water that piled up in the western Pacific to flow back east in the form of a Kelvin wave. It also slows down the upwelling, limiting how much cold water can reach the surface. Traveling east along the equator, the Kelvin wave hits Peru and Ecuador first before bouncing off the coast and moving north toward British Columbia and south toward Chile. The phenomenon causes temporary sea level rise, usually between 6 to 12 inches. We’re also in the midst of a “super” El Niño that’s expected to be one of the strongest on record because of how warm sea surface temperatures are getting. Temperatures in the eastern Pacific reached 5 degrees Celsius above normal on October 4th. “That is whopping big,” Seager says. “As you would expect for a big El Niño event, it’s going to be a big, powerful Kelvin wave.” Every inch of sea level rise can heighten the risk of flooding during storms and high tides. El Niño can push the North Pacific storm track southward, bringing more storms into Southern California, Seager explains. California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency in September to prepare for a particularly severe El Niño this season. Rising sea levels with climate change are already inundating seaside roads, railways, and neighborhoods in California. “If you already don’t have a lot of infrastructure that is built to protect your community and your coastline, you’re going to feel it … because 6 to 12 inches is not trivial,” says Emily Yam, senior director of learning and public engagement at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach, California. The extra warm water also has consequences for marine life. El Niño can be an exciting time to go fishing and whale watching, with many warm water-loving species traveling farther north than they typically would. NOAA notes that a 151-pound striped marlin broke a state record when it was caught in August off the coast of Washington. There have also been unusual sightings of hammerhead sharks and devil rays recently in Southern California. Unfortunately, hotter temperatures also put stress on coastal ecosystems. Yam says scientists are bracing for a potential die off of California’s iconic kelp forests. They thrive in temperatures around 50 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit, but the water has reached well into the 70s lately. The Kelvin wave is piling hot water into an area already suffering from a marine heatwave since May of last year. The temporary sea level rise is expected to linger through the start of winter. El Niño, which began in June, is forecast to weaken rapidly going into 2027.

articles.title: Type One Energy raised $200M to build a fusion power plant by 2034 | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Type One Energy is betting that its lean approach to fusion power will get a power plant on the grid faster, and investors have rewarded it with $200 million.
articles.body:
Type One Energy , a Knoxville, Tennessee-based startup founded in 2019 to build fusion power plants, announced Tuesday morning that it has raised $200 million from investors.

The funding helps the startup move up the ranks of the top-funded fusion power companies . But fusion is a costly field to work in. It sits at the cutting edge of plasma physics, materials science, and advanced computation, and even $200 million doesn’t always go far.

Even so, the new Series B should get the company halfway to paying for a 400-megawatt commercial power plant, Type One CEO Christofer Mowry told TechCrunch. If Type One can bring it online by 2034, he added, the company could complete its first power plant using less capital than many of its competitors, even with one or more subsequent rounds of funding.

The secret, Mowry said, is Type One’s business model. The company will design the power plant and many of its components, then turn to a “bespoke” network of suppliers chosen for the project to build them, he said. Most fusion startups rely on suppliers for some components, but Type One plans to go further.

That approach keeps costs down. “The amount of capital that we need to raise to commercialize fusion at Type One is just a different order of magnitude than if you were going to be vertically integrated,” Mowry said, referring to companies that make most of their own parts in-house.

“Why would I want to spend on bricks and mortar?” he added. “I used to run a big nuclear manufacturing company. That’s expensive.”

The fusion startup has already started assembling a roster of partners. Type One will build its first two fusion devices on the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run site, and infrastructure consultant AECOM is working on engineering for Infinity Two, the initial commercial power plant. Competitor Commonwealth Fusion Systems has licensed its high-temperature superconducting magnet technology to Type One, and the technology will help form the backbone of Type One’s reactor design.

By relying on outside suppliers, Type One becomes what’s known as an integrator, a company that assembles a product from parts made by others. That minimizes its own risk from activities like manufacturing, but it introduces a different kind of risk.

The upside is access to partners that may have more expertise in certain areas, like AECOM, the infrastructure consultant working on Infinity Two. “They have 10,000 people, most of them are engineers of one kind. We’re never going to have 10,000 people,” Mowry said.

The downside is that integrators have less control over their suppliers than an in-house team does. The most famous recent example might be Boeing, which relied on Spirit AeroSystems to supply fuselage sections for the 737 and 787 airliners. After a series of quality-control failures, including a door plug blowing out on an Alaska Airlines flight in 2024, Boeing bought Spirit, bringing it in-house to improve standards.

Type One is betting that it can manage the integration risk, and that it will be lower than the risk of doing everything in house. “These business models are successful because they let companies focus on managing risk and developing a high level of competency in their slice of the value chain,” Mowry said.

The round was led by repeat investor Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital. The company had previously raised $82.5 million in an extended Series A.

articles.title: Meet Andrew Sun-Zhuang, the Washington baseball player who built a $260 AI pitching machine with 94% strike accuracy and reached a national STEM final
articles.summary: Andrew Sun-Zhuang, a 7th grader at The Evergreen School in Shoreline, Washington, plays baseball and is constantly trying to improve his batting
articles.body: Andrew Sun-Zhuang, a 7th grader at The Evergreen School in Shoreline, Washington, plays baseball and is constantly trying to improve his batting performance. His hit rate is 95 per cent against a batting machine but only 35 per cent in real life. According to the Society for Science, he decided to train an AI to produce a better pitching machine. Using a Raspberry Pi, a camera, servos and motors, he built VisionStrike, a portable AI-powered pitching machine. It pitched with 86 per cent accuracy within a strike zone for front-toss pitching and threw fastball strikes with 94 per cent accuracy. The final prototype cost only $260.How did Andrew build the $260 AI pitching machineAndrew began by building his own pitching machine. He used a microcontroller, a Raspberry Pi, a camera, servos and motors. The Raspberry Pi later ran the AI model that controls the machine. For the AI itself, Andrew trained a model on 200 different pictures of a batter, himself. The model detected six key points on every image: the end of the bat, the wrist, elbow, shoulder, hip and knee. The model used these points to determine where the bat strike zone should be.Once the model is loaded onto the Raspberry Pi, it calculates the right angle after a batter has stood still for two seconds, according to the project description. The machine then launches the ball. This allows the machine to vary pitch location based on the batter, which Andrew identified as the missing feature in other pitching machines.The results were measured in two settings. The machine pitched with 86 per cent accuracy within the strike zone for front-toss pitching. For fastball pitching, it "threw" strikes with 94 per cent accuracy and balls with 97 per cent accuracy.How much did Andrew’s final AI pitching machine prototype costAndrew's final prototype cost only $260. The project description states that this is a major improvement over pitching machines, which usually cost much more. Baseball has been part of Andrew's life since he was five, when he started in Little League. Last summer, he played both All-Star Majors baseball and water polo. "I love baseball because of the connections I build with my teammates and the challenges I face during games," he says. "The pressure of competition pushes me to stay focused, build resilience, and constantly strive to become a better player." Andrew also enjoys robotics and has taken part in several robotics programmes. "I have a deep passion for robotics because it is an active, hands-on blend of STEM that can solve real-world problems," he says.

articles.title: Why Nobel winner physicist Francis Halzen built a giant ice cube to catch 'ghost particles'
articles.summary: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 has been awarded to a Belgian particle physicist, Prof Francis Halzen, for his fundamental contribution to establishing an
articles.body: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 has been awarded to a Belgian particle physicist, Prof Francis Halzen, for his fundamental contribution to establishing an enormous ice block observatory in the South Pole that detects neutrinos, the ghost particles from outer space.Let us understand what these ghost particles are and why Halzen's contribution is so relevantWhat are 'ghost' particlesThe neutrino is a tiny subatomic particle that has no charge. It weighs so little that its mass couldn't be measured yet. However, they are the most abundant particles, with a mass, in the universe.They are generated whenever atomic nuclei fuse, as occurs in the Sun, or split apart, as occurs in a fission reactor or a particle accelerator.These "ghost particles" are elusive and almost never interact with other matter. In fact, trillions of neutrinos from the Sun stream through our body every second, but we can’t feel them.Since the neutrinos are not affected by the magnetic field, they travel without deviation and hence can be traced back towards the source. So a neutrino essentially a messenger that carries information about its powerful place of origin.However, this is only possible if the neutrinos can be detected. This is where Halzen's contribution becomes relevant.Antarctica's massive ice cube observatoryThough extremely rare, when a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the clear glacial ice, detecting the presence of a neutrino.In 1988, Halzen presented his idea of capturing these ghost particles at the South Pole. A laboratory at the South Pole was proposed owing to several advantages offered by the location.Antarctica's ice is extremely clear and is also free from any kind of interference. The location is geologically stable, with no earthquakes.The IceCube neutrino observatory recorded the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, after it began operating in 2011.To construct it, scientists, technicians and engineers placed thousands of basketball-sized light sensors within a cubic kilometre of ice to pick up the faint flashes of light that can occur as neutrinos from space collide with atomic nuclei.The massive one-kilometre cube observation area is used because scientists need an enormous volume of material to increase the odds that a neutrino will occasionally smash into an atomic nucleus.“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision have paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” said Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics.

articles.title: Two lethal doses failed to kill Christa Pike. The science behind a botched US execution
articles.summary: For more than three decades, May Martinez lived with the same date burned into her memory: January 1995, when her 19-year-old daughter, Colleen Slemmer,
articles.body: For more than three decades, May Martinez lived with the same date burned into her memory: January 1995, when her 19-year-old daughter, Colleen Slemmer, was tortured and murdered.On September 30 this year, Martinez travelled 11 hours from Florida to Tennessee with her husband to witness what she believed would finally be the closing chapter. Christa Pike, the woman convicted of killing her daughter, was scheduled to die by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.Pike was 18 when she killed Slemmer. Now 50, she was about to become the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.Martinez and her husband arrived at about 8:30 in the morning and waited nearly 12 hours inside the prison before the death chamber finally opened.Inside the chamber, Pike was strapped to a gurney. An IV had been placed in her arm. A spiritual adviser stood near her head, speaking softly to her. They sang together. Pike smiled, raised her head and looked around.Martinez stood behind the glass with a photograph of Colleen. “I stood in front of that window, and I watched her very, very carefully. I did not take my eyes off of her,” Martinez later said. She wanted Pike to remember the young woman whose life had ended three decades earlier.At around 7.37 pm, the execution began.The botched executionPentobarbital, a powerful barbiturate that Tennessee uses as its sole lethal-injection drug, was administered through the IV.But Pike did not die. Witnesses heard her make snoring sounds.Shocked officials huddled to discuss the unprecedented situation before finally deciding to administer a second dose.But Pike remained alive.The scene had become an extraordinary inversion of what a modern execution is supposed to be: controlled, clinical and final. Instead of a body being taken away for burial, an ambulance was summoned. Instead of the state declaring a death, Pike was transported to a hospital for emergency medical treatment.And May Martinez left without the ending she had travelled hundreds of miles and waited decades to witness. “I broke down in tears,” Martinez later said, describing the moment she watched Pike lying on the table, talking, laughing and lifting her head. “I think that the state owes me a big apology.”A haunting questionSince the botched execution, Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator.And a critical question now haunts Tennessee.How could a procedure designed to make killing appear precise, medical and almost mechanical unravel so completely.The precise reason for the failed execution remains under investigation. Pike's lawyers say problems with the IV lines meant the pentobarbital entered surrounding tissue instead of the bloodstream. They had previously warned courts about difficulties accessing her veins.The Tennessee department of correction, however, has said its personnel followed the state's execution protocol.The fallout has already reached the top of Tennessee’s prison system. Governor Bill Lee has halted executions in the state for the remainder of 2026 and appointed former US attorney Ed Stanton to independently review what happened.Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada will resign later this month.What is the Colleen Slemmer case?On a January night in 1995 at Knoxville’s Job Corps Center in Tennessee, 18-year-old Christa Pike, her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and another student, Shadolla Peterson, attacked 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Prosecutors said the killing was an act of jealous rage triggered by romantic conflict.According to court records, the assault lasted roughly 30 to 45 minutes and involved repeated cutting, blows to Slemmer’s head and the carving of a pentagram into her chest. The brutality of the crime shocked Knoxville.Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. The jury found that the murder involved torture or serious physical abuse beyond what was necessary to cause death.Pike was sentenced to death, becoming one of the youngest women in the US to be sent to death row. After several rounds of appeals Pike's execution was ultimately scheduled for September 30, 2026.What exactly is lethal injection?Lethal injection is not one fixed recipe.Dr Thirunavukkarasu Sivaraman, lead consultant – Anaesthesiology & Pain Management at the SPARSH Hospital in Bengaluru said, “The three-substance injection technique was initially aimed at bringing unconsciousness followed by paralysis of respiratory muscles and finally the heart stopping. Other states have chosen to adopt the one-substance injection that involves the administration of a substance called pentobarbital with the intention of causing extreme CNS depression followed by respiratory arrest and finally death. This process is not supposed to induce painlessness but rather pain.The modern US era began in Texas. Charles Brooks Jr was executed by lethal injection on December 7, 1982, using sodium thiopental.The method was conceived as a more clinical alternative to execution by electrocution, and its supporters presented it as a swift and humane method.But the procedure depends on something deceptively basic: getting the drug into the bloodstream.So how can a lethal injection fail?A lethal drug can only have its intended systemic effect if it is delivered correctly. One potential problem is intravenous access. If a needle or catheter is not properly positioned in a vein, medication can enter the surrounding tissue instead of circulating through the bloodstream. A vein can also rupture, collapse or become unusable during the procedure.That is particularly significant in Pike’s case because her lawyers have specifically alleged problems with the IV lines. Her former lawyer James Crowson told The Guardian that previous legal filings had raised concerns about Pike’s veins and that he was not surprised the procedure encountered difficulties.The problem is not unique to PikeAccording to the Death Penalty Information Center, 51 US lethal-injection executions since 1976 have been classified as botched, including seven halted because officials could not establish an IV line. Before Christa Pike, no prisoner in the modern era was known to have survived after lethal-injection drugs were administered. Seven others survived failed attempts, but in each case, no drugs were given. Clayton Lockett’s 2014 Oklahoma execution bore similarities, though he died of a heart attack in the execution chamber.In Tennessee, the issue had surfaced before Pike. In May, officials halted the execution of Tony Carruthers after they were unable to establish a secondary IV line.Does two doses mean the drug did not work?Not necessarily.The failure of an execution does not establish that pentobarbital itself was ineffective. Investigators have to determine how much drug entered Pike’s bloodstream, how much may have entered surrounding tissue and whether the execution protocol was followed correctly.That distinction is crucial.A drug can be pharmacologically capable of causing death while a particular administration fails because delivery is compromised. In Pike’s case, however, officials have not publicly established what happened to the two doses.Dr Sivaraman said, “The number of times a drug is injected does not determine the amount of the active ingredient in the bloodstream. In case the IV tubing drips outside the blood vessel, the drug may fail to be absorbed, thus causing injury to the affected tissues. This would mean that giving the drug another time would result in additional injury with no visible results since it did not have the immediate effects.”The independent review ordered by Governor Lee is expected to examine precisely that question: whether Tennessee followed its protocol and whether changes are needed.How often do executions go wrong?More often than the image of a controlled, clinical procedure might suggest.Research by Austin Sarat covering US executions from 1890 to 2010 found 276 botched executions among 8,776 executions - about 3.15%. Lethal injection had the highest botch rate among the methods examined: 75 out of 1,054 executions, or 7.2%.A botched execution does not necessarily mean the prisoner survives.Dr Manish Bharti, head of Critical Care Medicine, Anaesthesiology and Critical Care, Metro Group of Hospitals, Pike’s case could be due to insufficient administration of the medication or an interruption in the delivery process. He added, “Severe barbiturate poisoning can be reversible with emergency interventions such as ventilation. However, being alive does not necessarily mean the individual has fully recovered, as prolonged unconsciousness, lack of oxygen and associated injuries can cause long-term effects.”The Death Penalty Information Center says lethal injection has remained particularly vulnerable to complications involving intravenous access, changing drug protocols and difficulty obtaining execution drugs.The problem has not disappeared. The DPIC said seven of 19 US execution attempts in 2022 were botched, although the sample was small.Why has lethal injection become more complicated?The original drug model has become difficult to sustain.Pharmaceutical companies have increasingly restricted the use of their medicines in executions, making it harder for states to obtain some traditional drugs. States have consequently changed protocols, switched drugs and, in some cases, relied on compounding pharmacies.“This is a case that requires an independent and transparent inquiry to take place before any conclusions are reached or other executions take place”, said Dr Bharti, while also raising concerns about the recipe used in the preparation of the lethal drugs. He said, "Another concern is the issue of secrecy regarding the personnel and the process involved, making it hard for an independent check on the process. Tennessee had earlier conducted a study where there were violations of their own protocol."The Death Penalty Information Center says these drug shortages and changes have contributed to legal challenges and prolonged executions, while secrecy laws in many states make it difficult for the public to know where execution drugs came from or how their quality was assessed.That has produced an unusual situation: a procedure designed to look medically precise is increasingly being carried out under rules that keep significant parts of the process away from public scrutiny.Is lethal injection the most common method?In the US, yes.The Death Penalty Information Center records 1,488 US executions by lethal injection since 1976 and says 28 states, along with the US government and military, authorise it.But lethal injection is not the only method available. Nine states authorise electrocution. Nine authorise some form of lethal gas, including nitrogen gas. Five, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, authorise firing squads.Nitrogen gas has emerged as a relatively new US execution method. Alabama carried out the first nitrogen-gas execution in 2024, and Louisiana has since also used the method.Tennessee itself permits electrocution as an alternative under certain circumstances, and the Pike case has already prompted Republican lawmakers to discuss expanding execution options.What happens in other countries?Lethal injection is used far less widely worldwide than the US association with the method might suggest.Amnesty International recorded executions in 17 countries in 2025. The methods used included lethal injection, hanging, shooting, beheading and nitrogen gas asphyxiation.The US was responsible for 47 recorded executions in 2025. China remained the world's largest executioner, although its figures are classified as a state secret. Amnesty also records extensive use of capital punishment in Iran and Saudi Arabia.And India?India retains the death penalty but does not use lethal injection. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, provides that a death sentence is carried out by hanging “by the neck till he is dead”.The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that capital punishment should be reserved for the “rarest of rare” cases.India therefore sits outside the US debate over lethal injection itself, although the broader question - how the state should carry out an irreversible punishment- remains relevant to any capital-punishment system.
